transcript.text: Shark NZ801UK anti hair wrap upright - suction has gone really weak over the last couple of weeks, barely picks up crumbs. Have emptied the bin. Any ideas before I buy a new one?

Before you spend money on a replacement, there is a very high probability that this issue can be fixed. The Shark NZ801UK (and most Shark uprights) relies heavily on airflow to generate suction. If the bin is empty but suction is weak, something else in the air path is blocked.

Here’s a step-by-step troubleshooting guide, ordered from easiest/most likely to more complex:

### 1. Check the "Anti-Allergy" Filter (Most Common Cause)
Shark vacuums have two main filters: one at the top of the bin and one at the back near the motor. If either is clogged with dust, suction drops dramatically.
• Top Filter: Located inside the bin lid. Remove it and rinse under cold water until the water runs clear. Let it dry for 24 hours completely before reinserting. Do not use soap or put it in a dishwasher.
• Rear Motor Filter: Located at the back of the vacuum, near where the power cord plugs in. Remove it and check for dust buildup. If it’s washable (check your manual), rinse it cold and let it dry for 24 hours. If it’s foam-only and looks grey/black/clogged, consider replacing it.

### 2. Inspect the Hose and Wand for Blockages
Even if the bin is empty, debris can get stuck in the hose or wand.
• Detach the hose from both ends (handle end and floor head end).
• Shine a torch through the hose to check for blockages.
• Use a long, flexible object (like a broom handle) to gently push any obstructions out.
• Check the wand itself – sometimes small debris gets stuck in the twist-lock mechanism or at the base of the wand.

### 3. Check the Brush Roll Area
The NZ801UK has an "Anti-Hair Wrap" brush bar, but it’s not foolproof. Hair and threads can still wrap around the ends or get tangled in the bristles, restricting airflow through the floor head.
• Flip the vacuum over.
• Remove the brush roll (usually by pressing a release button or sliding a latch).
• Clean out any hair, string, or debris from the brush bar and the inlet where air enters above the brush.

### 4. Check the Seals and Gaskets
If any seals are cracked, misaligned, or dirty, air leaks in, which kills suction.
• Inspect the rubber seal around the bin lid. Is it clean? Is it seated properly?
• Check the connection points between the hose, wand, and floor head. Ensure they click into place firmly.

### 5. Listen to the Motor Sound
• If the motor sounds normal (steady hum) but suction is weak: You have a blockage or filter issue (go back to steps 1–4).
• If the motor sounds strained, high-pitched, or weaker than usual: The motor itself may be failing, or there’s an internal blockage near the motor fan.

### 6. Reset the Vacuum
Sometimes the electronics can glitch. Unplug the vacuum for 5–10 minutes to let it reset, then try again.

---

### If None of This Works:
• Check Warranty: Shark typically offers a 2-year warranty in the UK. Check your purchase receipt or register your product on the Shark website. If it’s within warranty, contact Shark Customer Support for a repair or replacement.
• Contact Shark Support: They are generally very responsive. Describe the issue exactly as you did here: "Suction has gradually decreased over weeks despite emptying bin and cleaning filters."

Most likely fix: A clogged or wet rear filter. If you recently washed it, ensure it was completely dry before putting it back. Even slight moisture can severely restrict airflow.

Try these steps first – 90% of the time, this resolves weak suction on Shark vacuums.

Hose and wand are clear, seal looks fine, and the brushroll spins freely with a bit of fluff. Motor sounds normal, maybe slightly higher pitched. No burning smell. I've never washed any filters though, so I'm not sure where to look for them.

The fact that the motor sounds normal (even if slightly higher-pitched) and there’s no burning smell is a good sign—it means the motor itself isn’t failing or overheating. The "higher pitch" usually just indicates it’s working harder against resistance, which strongly points to an airflow blockage.

Since you’ve never washed the filters, this is almost certainly your problem. Shark vacuums rely on clean filters to maintain suction. If they’re clogged with fine dust, the vacuum essentially chokes itself.

Here’s exactly where to find and how to clean them on your NZ801UK:

### 1. The Pre-Motor Filter (Inside the Bin)
This is the most common culprit for sudden suction loss.
• Location: Open the bin lid fully. You’ll see a white, rectangular filter panel at the top of the bin, just inside the lid mechanism. It’s often labeled "Washable Filter."
• How to Clean:
• Remove it carefully.
• Rinse it under cold running water until the water runs clear (this may take a few minutes). Do not use soap or hot water.
• Shake off excess water and let it air-dry for at least 24 hours. This is critical—if you put it back damp, it will mold and cause odors/moldiness later.

### 2. The Post-Motor Filter (At the Back of the Vacuum)
This filter protects the motor from fine dust. If it’s clogged, suction drops significantly.
• Location: Look at the back of the vacuum body, near where the power cord plugs in. There’s a small flap or cover (sometimes held by a clip or screw). Remove this cover to reveal a white foam or felt filter.
• How to Clean:
• Check if your manual says it’s washable (most Shark post-motor filters are). If so, rinse gently under cold water until clean.
• Let it dry for 24 hours before reinstalling.
• Note: If the filter looks torn, disintegrated, or is made of paper-like material that can’t be washed, you’ll need to replace it (they’re cheap and available online).

### Why This Matters:
Shark vacuums are designed with a safety feature: if airflow is restricted too much, suction drops dramatically to protect the motor. Cleaning these filters will likely restore 80–90% of your suction immediately.

Next Steps:
1. Wash both filters (if washable) and let them dry for 24 hours.
2. Reassemble everything.
3. Test the vacuum.

If suction is still weak after this, try one more thing: Check the "Anti-Hair Wrap" brush bar again. Even though it spins freely, ensure there’s no dense mat of hair or string wrapped under the bristles or around the end caps that might be restricting airflow into the floor head. You can use scissors to carefully cut away any tangled debris.

Let me know how you get on after cleaning the filters!
Found them under the bin. The felt one was caked with fine dust. Washed both and left them to dry for 24 hours. Suction is back to like new, massive difference.

That’s fantastic news! It’s a classic case of "choked airflow"—once those filters were clear, the vacuum could breathe again. The fact that you caught it early also means you’ve likely extended the life of your motor significantly.

Since you’re back in business, here are two quick tips to keep this from happening again:

• Set a Reminder: Mark your calendar for 3–6 months from now to check and wash those filters again. Regular maintenance is much easier than dealing with a complete loss of suction later.
• Check the Bin Seal: While you’re at it, occasionally wipe down the rubber seal around the bin opening. A little dust buildup there can sometimes cause minor air leaks that reduce efficiency over time.

Enjoy the renewed power! If you ever notice the suction dropping again, you’ll know exactly where to look first.
